Question two. What is a load balancer, and how does it distribute traffic? It sits in front of the pool and spreads requests, so no one server is overwhelmed. Round-robin deals them in turn. Least-connections picks the server with the fewest open connections, which copes with slow requests. Consistent hashing sends a key to the same server every time, for servers that cache their own hot links. And health checks pull a dead server out of rotation, which is what makes a pool of stateless servers highly available. Why consistent? Simulate ten thousand short keys on three servers, by hash modulo three. Add a fourth, switch to modulo four, and seventy-four percent of the keys move, each one to a cold cache. On a hash ring, with a hundred points a server, only twenty-three percent move, all of them to the new server.

Question three. Explain the cache-aside pattern. On a read, the app checks the cache. On a miss, it reads the database, writes the value into the cache, and returns it. A write updates the database and invalidates the cached copy. Only what's asked for gets cached, and a cache failure falls through to the database, but every key's first request pays the miss. Simulate two million redirects over a million links, where a few links get most of the clicks. A cache holding a thousandth of the links answers forty percent. A hundredth, fifty-eight. A tenth, seventy-seven. And the better it works, the harder losing it lands: a dead cache multiplies the database's reads by two point four at fifty-eight percent, and by more than four at seventy-seven. So the cache needs replicas too.
